column1: # Consumer CPU generations, in release order.
#   vendor   Intel | AMD, matching what detect_cpu_vendor prints
#   ordinal  position in the release sequence, 1 = oldest listed
#   label    what the generation is called in the market
#   year     the year the generation launched, not the year a given part did
# The ordinal exists because "how many generations behind am I" is the question this
# table answers, and the marketing names cannot be subtracted: Intel ran 1st through
# 14th Gen and then restarted at "Core Ultra Series 1", and AMD's Ryzen model numbers
# skip (there is no mainstream desktop 4000 or 6000 series). An ordinal sequence is the
# **The newest row in this file defines "latest".** Nothing hardcodes it, so adding a
# generation is one line and every "N behind" recalculates. The consequence of *not*
# adding it is that the count silently under-reports — which is why the dashboard names
# the generation it is comparing against instead of only printing a number, and why
# Server lines (Xeon Scalable, EPYC) are deliberately absent: they have their own naming
# and do not sit on this ladder. A part whose microarchitecture has no generation maps
# to `-` in cpu-arch.tsv and the dashboard says so.
# That line means someone ran scripts/refresh-cpu-generations.sh and compared this table
# against ark.intel.com and amd.com on that date. It is not the date the file was last
# edited — an earlier version of this header recorded that instead, which made the table
# look current when nothing had ever been checked against a source.
# Sources, and what each is good for:
#   Intel  ark.intel.com lists every processor family it knows, and each family's series
#          page carries per-SKU launch quarters. The earliest quarter in a series is when
#          so the highest /ryzen/NNNN-series/ path is the newest desktop family. The
#          specification browser is a JS application with no documented data endpoint,
#          so per-SKU dates come from individual product pages.
